content_html:
Signal now offers a feature called “automatic key verification” which complements the existing safety number system. Signal is always end-to-end encrypted, and automatic key verification provides an additional, streamlined way to confirm that there’s no unexpected party between you and the other “end” of an end-to-end encrypted session.

It works through a system of verifications performed by you, your Signal connections, and third-party auditors that together provide the same assurance as manually verifying safety numbers. Unlike safety numbers, these verifications are done independently and do not require an in-person meeting or a secondary communication channel.

This system of verifications ensures that the association between a phone number or username and its public encryption key is globally consistent and transparent to all participants in Signal’s ecosystem. This protects against scenarios where a key is swapped out without the key owner’s knowledge — for example, if a malicious party compromised Signal and associated a different key with your connection’s phone number.

To see this feature in action, go to a Signal connection’s profile, hit “View Safety Number,” and tap on the “Verify automatically” button under the “Automatic key verification” heading. The button will show a green checkmark and “Encryption verified” when the feature is available and verification succeeds. Over time, this verification, combined with the ones continually performed by your Signal connection and third-party auditors, ensures the consistency of this Signal connection’s key across the Signal ecosystem.

This feature is built on a concept known as “key transparency,” which is the term we’ll use throughout the rest of this post as we explain why we built a key transparency system and give a high-level overview of how it works.

A primer on public and private keys

Asymmetric cryptography is what enables you to send messages to your friend that only your friend can read. It involves a pair of mathematically-linked keys called the public key and private key, which can be used in a variety of applications including sending and receiving messages.

Imagine you have a locked mailbox with a slot. Your public key is like your mailbox address — you can share it with anyone who wants to send mail to you. Your private key is like the mailbox key. You’re the only person that has it, and you can use it to read messages sent to you. Anyone can drop mail in your mailbox (encrypt with your public key), but only you can unlock and read it (decrypt with your private key). Your mailbox address must be publicly available; you can’t receive mail if no one knows where to send it.

When you sign up for Signal, the Signal app generates a public/private key pair for you as part of the registration process1. The private key stays on your device — only you, not Signal, not anyone else, have access to this private key. Your public key is sent to Signal, which acts as a central directory for all users’ public keys. When you want to send a message to another Signal user, you ask Signal for your connection’s public key and encrypt your message with the key that Signal hands back and your private key.

Mallory in the middle attack

Sending messages requires fetching public keys for recipients, and fetching public keys means relying on a central directory. In theory, a malicious directory operator could carry out something called a “Mallory in the middle” attack, though doing so would require an outsider bypassing the security of major cloud providers or a privileged insider deliberately targeting a specific account. But even though this is a very advanced and unlikely attack, it’s one we still want to guard against. We’ll continue using the mailbox analogy to illustrate how this attack would hypothetically work.

Imagine Bob wants to send an invitation for coffee to his friend Alice, so Bob looks up her mailbox address in the central directory. If the directory is somehow compromised by an adversary (Mallory), it might direct Bob to Mallory’s mailbox instead of Alice’s. When Bob sends his mail to what he thinks is Alice’s mailbox, it actually goes to Mallory’s mailbox instead. Mallory then uses her own mailbox key to retrieve Bob’s message, reads it, modifies it if she chooses, puts it in a new envelope, and forwards it to Alice’s mailbox.

In her modification, Mallory could change the coffee shop location or meeting time for example, causing Alice to show up at the wrong place or time. Alice would have no indication that the message had been intercepted or tampered with, so to her, it looks like the message came directly from Bob. Meanwhile, Bob would be left waiting fruitlessly for Alice to show up. And even if Mallory chose not to alter Bob’s message, her ability to read it at all constitutes a serious breach of communication privacy.

Miscommunication about coffee is relatively low-stakes, but this kind of attack can create far more harm in other contexts.

This attack works because Bob never actually verified Alice’s address. Bob just trusted that the mailbox listed in the directory is hers, which is a reasonable assumption.

But, if Bob wanted to be extra cautious, he could ask Alice for her address directly either through an in-person meeting or some secondary, trusted communication channel2, which may not be feasible if Alice and Bob are strictly pen pals.

So, how does Bob verify Alice’s address if he cannot meet her in person or use a secondary channel?

In the rest of this blog post, we’ll outline how we developed a design for a system that enables Bob to automatically verify the data in the central directory without needing to communicate with Alice directly.

An analogy for designing a key transparency system

One way we could help Bob verify that the directory has the correct address for Alice is to keep a record of every change ever made to the directory. If somebody changes Alice’s address in the directory, it will be captured in this chronological log and therefore detectable. To make this concrete, let’s extend the mailbox analogy.

Let’s say a clerk records everyone’s address changes in a public ledger in the city post office. Whenever anyone gets a new address or updates an existing one, the clerk adds a new page to the back of the ever-growing ledger and records the address change there. The clerk does so with a permanent marker so that once something is written, nobody can go back to a page and rip it out or modify its contents. Anyone can visit the post office and find an address in the ledger, including their own.

Using the ledger

For any given address, there are two ways for post office customers to interact with the ledger:

  1. A customer like Bob can look up addresses for other people (like Alice).
  2. A customer like Alice can look up her own address to ensure that the ledger is accurate.

For Bob to find Alice’s current address, he would have to start at the last ledger page and flip back one page at a time until he finds a page for Alice. Bob starts at the end of the ledger and works backwards because he wants Alice’s most recent address, and Alice’s address may have changed over time. As more pages are added to the ledger, this can become a lot of work for Bob, especially if Alice hasn’t updated her address in a while and there are lots of address changes for other people that Bob needs to sift through.

The ledger allows Alice to verify that her own address is listed correctly, but in order to do so she has to look at all of the new pages since her last visit and check that they never misstate her address. Like Bob, this becomes a lot of work as more pages are added to the ledger.

If Alice and Bob live in a busy city where people frequently change addresses, they would both have to do a prohibitive amount of work to use the ledger by flipping through one page at a time. We need a more efficient way for Alice and Bob to interact with the ledger.

Introducing index books

In real life, books often contain an alphabetically sorted index that allows readers to quickly locate what they’re looking for. We can apply that same idea to our ledger by introducing an alphabetically sorted index book over the names of every person whose address has been included in the ledger so far.

As new pages are added to the ledger to reflect new addresses or address changes, the index book must update too, so the clerk publishes a new copy of the index book every time they add a page to the ledger, containing the set of people whose addresses have been included in the ledger as of that page. This creates a huge library of all past index books that are available to the public.

For now, let us assume that Alice and Bob are always looking at the same index book for any given page of the ledger. In the next section, we’ll discuss another component of the system that allows Alice and Bob to verify this assumption.

With this construction, Bob can now more easily look up Alice’s address in the ledger via a “binary search” strategy, one that is best illustrated via a concrete example.

Let’s say that there have been 100 new or updated addresses over a period of time, so the ledger has 100 pages and the clerk has published 100 different editions of the index book. For simplicity, we will say that Alice’s address only appears once in the ledger, when she first moved to town.

Bob starts by flipping to the middle of the ledger. He then checks the index book associated with that page. The index book is alphabetically sorted so it’s easy to find a person’s name. If Alice’s name exists in that index book, then this is either the first edition of the index book that contains an entry for Alice or the first appearance is in an earlier edition and therefore an earlier page in the ledger.

In either case, Bob can ignore the back half of the ledger and repeat the process with the front half of the ledger until he finds the exact ledger page where Alice’s address change occurred. Specifically, Bob’s search will end when he finds two adjacent index books where the first one doesn’t contain Alice’s address and the second one does.

This search process has a few benefits, the first one being that it is efficient. In a ledger with a billion pages, instead of flipping backwards (in the worst case) through all billion pages, Bob only needs to examine 30 different pages at most to find Alice’s address. Bob’s job is now much easier than it was before.

Alice still wants to make sure that the clerk never adds any new pages that are wrong about her address. However, Alice doesn’t need to check every ledger page and index book. She just needs to check the same ones that Bob looked at to find her address, which ensures that the address Bob finds for Alice has been verified by Alice herself.

This brings us to the second benefit of the search process, which is that it is deterministic when Alice and Bob look at the ledger with the same number of pages. Things get more complicated if the clerk adds more pages between Bob’s and Alice’s searches, but the main idea remains the same. In a ledger with a billion pages, Alice can follow the same search process as Bob, check the same pages that Bob checked, and ensure that none of them contain wrong information about her address.

By agreeing to a process for searching through the ledger, Alice and Bob have established a way to interact with the ledger that enables them to practically achieve their respective goals. As the ledger continues to grow, Bob has an efficient way to find Alice’s address, and Alice has an efficient way to ensure that the address Bob finds is accurate.

This analogy is simplified for the sake of clarity. In practice, Alice can update her address multiple times, and supporting this kind of search requires storing more data in the index books than just names. We’ve built an open-source key transparency server that applies these same ideas to Signal messaging.

What about the clerk?

So far, we’ve described the search process as if Alice and Bob personally flip through the ledger pages and check the index books. In practice, that’s not realistic because the ledger and index books are too large for Alice or Bob to handle directly. Instead, Alice and Bob ask the clerk to perform the search on their behalf and report back the results.

But the post office could be compromised by an adversary like Mallory who poses as the clerk and who wants to ultimately trick Bob into thinking Alice’s address is actually Mallory’s home. As a result, Alice and Bob cannot simply trust the clerk; they must be able to independently verify the search process themselves.

To do so, they ask the clerk to hand back all the data from the specific ledger pages and index books that the clerk looked at during the search process, and they double-check the results themselves.

Double-checking only works if the data the clerk hands back can be trusted, which raises an obvious question: what if Mallory, posing as the clerk, lies about what the records say? For example, Mallory could maintain a secret, second ledger that records the wrong address for Alice or publish two different editions of an index book for the same ledger page. Mallory could provide data from one view to Alice and data from the other view to Bob, tricking them into verifying the provided data without realizing Mallory’s deception.

Alice and Bob need an independent witness to keep the clerk honest.

Third-party auditors

To prevent Mallory from providing different data to Alice and Bob, they rely on third-party auditors. These auditors are like notaries who watch over the clerk’s shoulder as the clerk adds each successive page to the ledger and publishes the corresponding index book edition.

They check that each edition of the index book contains all the same data as the previous edition with the exception of one entry, and that the auditor has not removed or otherwise secretly modified any previous pages in the ledger. If these conditions are true, the auditor signs3 that ledger page and index book, indicating that the record was added correctly.

Auditors will only ever sign each page and index book once, so if the clerk attempted to show different versions of the 50th edition of the index book to Alice and Bob, the clerk would only be able to produce a valid accompanying auditor signature for one of those versions. By checking for and verifying these auditor signatures, Alice and Bob can be assured that the clerk is maintaining exactly one ledger and corresponding set of index books, and that they therefore are looking at the same set of records.

For Signal’s implementation of key transparency, Cloudflare and Trail of Bits serve as trusted third-party auditors.

Monitoring

Third-party auditors ensure that the clerk provides the same set of data to Alice and Bob, but they can’t verify the accuracy of the recorded data. For example, Mallory could attempt to add a page to the ledger listing a fake address change for Alice. From an auditor’s perspective, this is a legitimate change as long as Mallory correctly adds a new ledger page and publishes a new edition of the index book. However, when Bob looks up Alice’s address in the ledger, he’ll find this fake entry and believe that it is Alice’s real address.

This is where monitoring comes in. Recall that there are two ways for customers to interact with the ledger: looking up someone else’s address, and looking up their own. Monitoring requires Alice and Bob to do both of these things on a regular basis, each detecting a different kind of tampering.

Alice monitors her own data in the ledger by periodically looking up and verifying her most recent address record. If she finds an unexpected address, she should alert Bob through a secondary, trusted channel that the address he received for her is untrustworthy.

Bob must also periodically look up Alice’s most recent address and check that it matches what he received previously. This matters because after inserting a fake address change, Mallory could try to cover her tracks by later adding an entry restoring Alice’s correct address.

It’s important to note that from Bob’s perspective, finding a different address for Alice looks identical to a legitimate address change, which is the far more common explanation. Still, he should confirm with Alice through the secondary channel that she actually moved. If she didn’t, he should treat the earlier address as untrustworthy.

Alice performs self-checks at a regular cadence and Bob checks the ledger on his own schedule, so neither is guaranteed to catch Mallory’s interference the moment it happens. But these two kinds of monitoring, combined with third-party auditing, form a complete detection system: auditing guarantees that Alice and Bob are looking at the same data, and monitoring guarantees that both of them are regularly checking that data for accuracy. Together, they ensure that tampering by Mallory will eventually be detected.

Tying it back to Signal

So, how does this all connect back to key transparency in Signal?

In Signal, you can choose to be discoverable by your phone number or by a username if you choose to create one. If you decide to be discoverable by phone number or username, someone can type your number or username into Signal to initiate a message request. Signal stores a central directory that ultimately maps these public identifiers to the user’s public key, just like the “name” and “address” from our mailbox analogy.

When Signal users register, change their phone number or username, or re-create their account, Signal records the changes in a log tree (“the ledger”) and facilitates searching through the log tree with prefix trees (“the index books”). Cloudflare and Trail of Bits each serve as independent auditors of these two types of trees, which together form the key transparency log.

All user data in the log is cryptographically obscured — public identifiers are processed through a verifiable random function and the values they map to are protected by a keyed hash function — so auditors never see any plaintext user data.

Your Signal app automatically and periodically checks your own public identifiers in this log, but verifying those of a connection must be initiated in the “View Safety Number” screen. All requests to look up identifiers in the log are unauthenticated, so they aren’t tied to a specific user account.

While we won’t dive into the implementation details in this post, interested readers can find them in our open-source repository, which was implemented based on an earlier draft of the IETF key transparency protocol and contains refinements to fit Signal’s use case.

Key transparency in practice today

Key transparency indicates that all devices in Signal’s ecosystem share the same view of the associations between an identifier and its public encryption key. It does not verify the identity of the user who controls a particular phone number or username. Concretely, this means that Alice and Bob can perform key transparency checks to ensure that they each have the right public key for a given account, but additional verification (such as following up after a Safety Number change) would still be necessary to detect a scenario where Mallory has fully taken control of Alice’s account.

Today, your Signal app automatically verifies your own phone number and username data in the log. But to verify this for someone else, you need to have their phone number. Meaning that if you connected with someone on Signal via username, and did not exchange phone numbers or otherwise have access to their phone number, you will not be able to verify them.

You probably have your Signal connection’s phone number if any of the following conditions are true:

  • You started a Signal chat with this person using the “Find by phone number” option.
  • You have this person’s contact saved in your phone’s address book (and they have opted to be discoverable by phone number in Signal).
  • Your connection selected the option that lets everyone see their phone number in Signal (by default, nobody can).

Keep in mind that Signal will only display a Signal connection’s phone number in the app if they are in your phone’s address book or if they have set their phone number visibility to everyone.

It’s also possible for you to have an out-of-date phone number in the case that your connection on Signal changes their phone number. This action has no security impact on your connection’s public encryption key and the underlying encrypted messaging session. But it does mean that you will not be able to use automatic key verification for this connection because your phone will continue to have your connection’s old phone number which will no longer match the most recent phone number record in the ledger. This is similar to the situation described in the monitoring section where Bob sees a different address for Alice than what he had previously received. It’s very likely a legitimate change, but your device can’t distinguish that from server interference, and you should follow up with your connection through a secondary, trusted channel.

As a privacy-focused default, we make automatic key verification unavailable in all of these cases and recommend that users use the existing safety number system, which allows users to manually verify that they share the same set of encryption keys with a specific connection by scanning a QR code or comparing a long verification number. Users who prefer not to rely on any third party, including Signal and the auditors, can disable the automatic key verification feature in the settings via “Privacy” > “Advanced” > “Automatic Key Verification” and continue to use manual safety number verification.

Conclusion

Key transparency offers an easy-to-use way to confirm an important part of messaging security, complementing our existing safety number system.

This work represents a significant collaboration within and outside of Signal, and we’re especially grateful to Cloudflare and Trail of Bits for serving as independent auditors. We thank them and the many other people in our ecosystem who make this work possible.

  1. In practice, Signal actually generates several different kinds of key pairs and derived keys that work together as part of the Signal protocol, rather than relying on a single public/private key pair. ↩

  2. On the Signal platform, this is analogous to our existing “Safety Number” feature, which requires an in-person verification or comparing safety numbers via a second, trusted platform. ↩

  3. In the physical world, signatures can be easily forged. But in the key transparency system that this analogy describes, Signal’s third-party auditors use cryptographic signatures, which cannot be easily forged. ↩

By checking for and verifying these auditor signatures, Alice and Bob can be assured that the clerk is maintaining exactly one ledger and corresponding set of index books, and that they therefore are looking at the same set of records.For Signal’s implementation of key transparency, Cloudflare and Trail of Bits serve as trusted third-party auditors.MonitoringThird-party auditors ensure that the clerk provides the same set of data to Alice and Bob, but they can’t verify the accuracy of the recorded data. For example, Mallory could attempt to add a page to the ledger listing a fake address change for Alice. From an auditor’s perspective, this is a legitimate change as long as Mallory correctly adds a new ledger page and publishes a new edition of the index book. However, when Bob looks up Alice’s address in the ledger, he’ll find this fake entry and believe that it is Alice’s real address.This is where monitoring comes in. Recall that there are two ways for customers to interact with the ledger: looking up someone else’s address, and looking up their own. Monitoring requires Alice and Bob to do both of these things on a regular basis, each detecting a different kind of tampering.Alice monitors her own data in the ledger by periodically looking up and verifying her most recent address record. If she finds an unexpected address, she should alert Bob through a secondary, trusted channel that the address he received for her is untrustworthy.Bob must also periodically look up Alice’s most recent address and check that it matches what he received previously. This matters because after inserting a fake address change, Mallory could try to cover her tracks by later adding an entry restoring Alice’s correct address.It’s important to note that from Bob’s perspective, finding a different address for Alice looks identical to a legitimate address change, which is the far more common explanation. Still, he should confirm with Alice through the secondary channel that she actually moved. If she didn’t, he should treat the earlier address as untrustworthy.Alice performs self-checks at a regular cadence and Bob checks the ledger on his own schedule, so neither is guaranteed to catch Mallory’s interference the moment it happens. But these two kinds of monitoring, combined with third-party auditing, form a complete detection system: auditing guarantees that Alice and Bob are looking at the same data, and monitoring guarantees that both of them are regularly checking that data for accuracy. Together, they ensure that tampering by Mallory will eventually be detected.Tying it back to SignalSo, how does this all connect back to key transparency in Signal?In Signal, you can choose to be discoverable by your phone number or by a username if you choose to create one. If you decide to be discoverable by phone number or username, someone can type your number or username into Signal to initiate a message request. Signal stores a central directory that ultimately maps these public identifiers to the user’s public key, just like the “name” and “address” from our mailbox analogy.When Signal users register, change their phone number or username, or re-create their account, Signal records the changes in a log tree (“the ledger”) and facilitates searching through the log tree with prefix trees (“the index books”). Cloudflare and Trail of Bits each serve as independent auditors of these two types of trees, which together form the key transparency log.All user data in the log is cryptographically obscured — public identifiers are processed through a verifiable random function and the values they map to are protected by a keyed hash function — so auditors never see any plaintext user data.Your Signal app automatically and periodically checks your own public identifiers in this log, but verifying those of a connection must be initiated in the “View Safety Number” screen. All requests to look up identifiers in the log are unauthenticated, so they aren’t tied to a specific user account.While we won’t dive into the implementation details in this post, interested readers can find them in our open-source repository, which was implemented based on an earlier draft of the IETF key transparency protocol and contains refinements to fit Signal’s use case.Key transparency in practice todayKey transparency indicates that all devices in Signal’s ecosystem share the same view of the associations between an identifier and its public encryption key. It does not verify the identity of the user who controls a particular phone number or username. Concretely, this means that Alice and Bob can perform key transparency checks to ensure that they each have the right public key for a given account, but additional verification (such as following up after a Safety Number change) would still be necessary to detect a scenario where Mallory has fully taken control of Alice’s account.Today, your Signal app automatically verifies your own phone number and username data in the log. But to verify this for someone else, you need to have their phone number. Meaning that if you connected with someone on Signal via username, and did not exchange phone numbers or otherwise have access to their phone number, you will not be able to verify them.You probably have your Signal connection’s phone number if any of the following conditions are true:You started a Signal chat with this person using the “Find by phone number” option.You have this person’s contact saved in your phone’s address book (and they have opted to be discoverable by phone number in Signal).Your connection selected the option that lets everyone see their phone number in Signal (by default, nobody can).Keep in mind that Signal will only display a Signal connection’s phone number in the app if they are in your phone’s address book or if they have set their phone number visibility to everyone.It’s also possible for you to have an out-of-date phone number in the case that your connection on Signal changes their phone number. This action has no security impact on your connection’s public encryption key and the underlying encrypted messaging session. But it does mean that you will not be able to use automatic key verification for this connection because your phone will continue to have your connection’s old phone number which will no longer match the most recent phone number record in the ledger. This is similar to the situation described in the monitoring section where Bob sees a different address for Alice than what he had previously received. It’s very likely a legitimate change, but your device can’t distinguish that from server interference, and you should follow up with your connection through a secondary, trusted channel.As a privacy-focused default, we make automatic key verification unavailable in all of these cases and recommend that users use the existing safety number system, which allows users to manually verify that they share the same set of encryption keys with a specific connection by scanning a QR code or comparing a long verification number. Users who prefer not to rely on any third party, including Signal and the auditors, can disable the automatic key verification feature in the settings via “Privacy” > “Advanced” > “Automatic Key Verification” and continue to use manual safety number verification.ConclusionKey transparency offers an easy-to-use way to confirm an important part of messaging security, complementing our existing safety number system.This work represents a significant collaboration within and outside of Signal, and we’re especially grateful to Cloudflare and Trail of Bits for serving as independent auditors. We thank them and the many other people in our ecosystem who make this work possible.In practice, Signal actually generates several different kinds of key pairs and derived keys that work together as part of the Signal protocol, rather than relying on a single public/private key pair. ↩On the Signal platform, this is analogous to our existing “Safety Number” feature, which requires an in-person verification or comparing safety numbers via a second, trusted platform. ↩In the physical world, signatures can be easily forged. But in the key transparency system that this analogy describes, Signal’s third-party auditors use cryptographic signatures, which cannot be easily forged. ↩

blocks.html_en: A primer on public and private keys

sentences.en: A primer on public and private keys

blocks.html_en: Asymmetric cryptography is what enables you to send messages to your friend that only your friend can read. It involves a pair of mathematically-linked keys called the public key and private key, which can be used in a variety of applications including sending and receiving messages.

blocks.html_en: Imagine you have a locked mailbox with a slot. Your public key is like your mailbox address — you can share it with anyone who wants to send mail to you. Your private key is like the mailbox key. You’re the only person that has it, and you can use it to read messages sent to you. Anyone can drop mail in your mailbox (encrypt with your public key), but only you can unlock and read it (decrypt with your private key). Your mailbox address must be publicly available; you can’t receive mail if no one knows where to send it.

blocks.html_en: When you sign up for Signal, the Signal app generates a public/private key pair for you as part of the registration process1. The private key stays on your device — only you, not Signal, not anyone else, have access to this private key. Your public key is sent to Signal, which acts as a central directory for all users’ public keys. When you want to send a message to another Signal user, you ask Signal for your connection’s public key and encrypt your message with the key that Signal hands back and your private key.

sentences.en: Mallory in the middle attack
sentences.zh: 马洛里中路进攻

blocks.html_en: Sending messages requires fetching public keys for recipients, and fetching public keys means relying on a central directory. In theory, a malicious directory operator could carry out something called a “Mallory in the middle” attack, though doing so would require an outsider bypassing the security of major cloud providers or a privileged insider deliberately targeting a specific account. But even though this is a very advanced and unlikely attack, it’s one we still want to guard against. We’ll continue using the mailbox analogy to illustrate how this attack would hypothetically work.

blocks.html_en: Imagine Bob wants to send an invitation for coffee to his friend Alice, so Bob looks up her mailbox address in the central directory. If the directory is somehow compromised by an adversary (Mallory), it might direct Bob to Mallory’s mailbox instead of Alice’s. When Bob sends his mail to what he thinks is Alice’s mailbox, it actually goes to Mallory’s mailbox instead. Mallory then uses her own mailbox key to retrieve Bob’s message, reads it, modifies it if she chooses, puts it in a new envelope, and forwards it to Alice’s mailbox.

blocks.html_en: One way we could help Bob verify that the directory has the correct address for Alice is to keep a record of every change ever made to the directory. If somebody changes Alice’s address in the directory, it will be captured in this chronological log and therefore detectable. To make this concrete, let’s extend the mailbox analogy.

blocks.html_en: Let’s say a clerk records everyone’s address changes in a public ledger in the city post office. Whenever anyone gets a new address or updates an existing one, the clerk adds a new page to the back of the ever-growing ledger and records the address change there. The clerk does so with a permanent marker so that once something is written, nobody can go back to a page and rip it out or modify its contents. Anyone can visit the post office and find an address in the ledger, including their own.

blocks.html_en: Third-party auditors ensure that the clerk provides the same set of data to Alice and Bob, but they can’t verify the accuracy of the recorded data. For example, Mallory could attempt to add a page to the ledger listing a fake address change for Alice. From an auditor’s perspective, this is a legitimate change as long as Mallory correctly adds a new ledger page and publishes a new edition of the index book. However, when Bob looks up Alice’s address in the ledger, he’ll find this fake entry and believe that it is Alice’s real address.

sentences.en: Third-party auditors ensure that the clerk provides the same set of data to Alice and Bob, but they can’t verify the accuracy of the recorded data.
sentences.zh: 第三方审计员确保店员向 Alice 和 Bob 提供同一组数据，但他们无法验证记录数据的准确性。

sentences.en: For example, Mallory could attempt to add a page to the ledger listing a fake address change for Alice.
sentences.zh: 例如，Mallory 可以尝试向分类帐添加一个页面，列出 Alice 的虚假地址更改。

sentences.en: From an auditor’s perspective, this is a legitimate change as long as Mallory correctly adds a new ledger page and publishes a new edition of the index book.
sentences.zh: 从审计师的角度来看，只要马洛里正确添加新的分类账页并发布新版本的索引书，这就是合法的更改。

sentences.en: However, when Bob looks up Alice’s address in the ledger, he’ll find this fake entry and believe that it is Alice’s real address.
sentences.zh: 然而，当鲍勃在账本中查找爱丽丝的地址时，他会发现这个假条目并相信这是爱丽丝的真实地址。

blocks.html_en: This is where monitoring comes in. Recall that there are two ways for customers to interact with the ledger: looking up someone else’s address, and looking up their own. Monitoring requires Alice and Bob to do both of these things on a regular basis, each detecting a different kind of tampering.

sentences.en: This is where monitoring comes in.
sentences.zh: 这就是监控发挥作用的地方。

sentences.en: Recall that there are two ways for customers to interact with the ledger: looking up someone else’s address, and looking up their own.
sentences.zh: 回想一下，客户有两种方式与账本交互：查找别人的地址，以及查找自己的地址。

sentences.en: Monitoring requires Alice and Bob to do both of these things on a regular basis, each detecting a different kind of tampering.
sentences.zh: 监控要求 Alice 和 Bob 定期执行这两件事，每个都检测不同类型的篡改。

blocks.html_en: Alice monitors her own data in the ledger by periodically looking up and verifying her most recent address record. If she finds an unexpected address, she should alert Bob through a secondary, trusted channel that the address he received for her is untrustworthy.

sentences.en: Alice monitors her own data in the ledger by periodically looking up and verifying her most recent address record.
sentences.zh: Alice 通过定期查找和验证她最近的地址记录来监控她自己在分类账中的数据。

sentences.en: If she finds an unexpected address, she should alert Bob through a secondary, trusted channel that the address he received for her is untrustworthy.
sentences.zh: 如果她发现一个意外的地址，她应该通过第二个可信渠道提醒鲍勃，他为她收到的地址不可信。

blocks.html_en: Bob must also periodically look up Alice’s most recent address and check that it matches what he received previously. This matters because after inserting a fake address change, Mallory could try to cover her tracks by later adding an entry restoring Alice’s correct address.

sentences.en: Bob must also periodically look up Alice’s most recent address and check that it matches what he received previously.
sentences.zh: 鲍勃还必须定期查找爱丽丝的最新地址，并检查它是否与他之前收到的地址相符。

sentences.en: This matters because after inserting a fake address change, Mallory could try to cover her tracks by later adding an entry restoring Alice’s correct address.
sentences.zh: 这很重要，因为在插入虚假地址更改后，马洛里可以尝试通过稍后添加恢复爱丽丝正确地址的条目来掩盖她的踪迹。

blocks.html_en: It’s important to note that from Bob’s perspective, finding a different address for Alice looks identical to a legitimate address change, which is the far more common explanation. Still, he should confirm with Alice through the secondary channel that she actually moved. If she didn’t, he should treat the earlier address as untrustworthy.

sentences.en: It’s important to note that from Bob’s perspective, finding a different address for Alice looks identical to a legitimate address change, which is the far more common explanation.
sentences.zh: 值得注意的是，从鲍勃的角度来看，为爱丽丝找到不同的地址看起来与合法的地址更改相同，这是更常见的解释。

sentences.en: Still, he should confirm with Alice through the secondary channel that she actually moved.
sentences.zh: 尽管如此，他还是应该通过辅助渠道向爱丽丝确认她确实搬家了。

sentences.en: If she didn’t, he should treat the earlier address as untrustworthy.
sentences.zh: 如果她不这样做，他应该将之前的地址视为不可信。

blocks.html_en: Alice performs self-checks at a regular cadence and Bob checks the ledger on his own schedule, so neither is guaranteed to catch Mallory’s interference the moment it happens. But these two kinds of monitoring, combined with third-party auditing, form a complete detection system: auditing guarantees that Alice and Bob are looking at the same data, and monitoring guarantees that both of them are regularly checking that data for accuracy. Together, they ensure that tampering by Mallory will eventually be detected.

sentences.en: But these two kinds of monitoring, combined with third-party auditing, form a complete detection system: auditing guarantees that Alice and Bob are looking at the same data, and monitoring guarantees that both of them are regularly checking that data for accuracy.

sentences.en: Together, they ensure that tampering by Mallory will eventually be detected.
sentences.zh: 他们共同确保马洛里的篡改最终会被发现。

blocks.html_en: Tying it back to Signal

sentences.en: Tying it back to Signal
sentences.zh: 将其绑定回 Signal

blocks.html_en: So, how does this all connect back to key transparency in Signal?

sentences.en: So, how does this all connect back to key transparency in Signal?
sentences.zh: 那么，这一切如何与 Signal 中的关键透明度联系起来呢？

blocks.html_en: In Signal, you can choose to be discoverable by your phone number or by a username if you choose to create one. If you decide to be discoverable by phone number or username, someone can type your number or username into Signal to initiate a message request. Signal stores a central directory that ultimately maps these public identifiers to the user’s public key, just like the “name” and “address” from our mailbox analogy.

sentences.en: In Signal, you can choose to be discoverable by your phone number or by a username if you choose to create one.
sentences.zh: 在 Signal 中，您可以选择通过电话号码或用户名（如果您选择创建用户名）来发现。

sentences.en: If you decide to be discoverable by phone number or username, someone can type your number or username into Signal to initiate a message request.
sentences.zh: 如果您决定通过电话号码或用户名被发现，其他人可以在 Signal 中输入您的号码或用户名来发起消息请求。

sentences.en: Signal stores a central directory that ultimately maps these public identifiers to the user’s public key, just like the “name” and “address” from our mailbox analogy.
sentences.zh: Signal 存储一个中央目录，最终将这些公共标识符映射到用户的公钥，就像我们邮箱类比中的“名称”和“地址”一样。

blocks.html_en: When Signal users register, change their phone number or username, or re-create their account, Signal records the changes in a log tree (“the ledger”) and facilitates searching through the log tree with prefix trees (“the index books”). Cloudflare and Trail of Bits each serve as independent auditors of these two types of trees, which together form the key transparency log.

sentences.en: When Signal users register, change their phone number or username, or re-create their account, Signal records the changes in a log tree (“the ledger”) and facilitates searching through the log tree with prefix trees (“the index books”).
sentences.zh: 当 Signal 用户注册、更改电话号码或用户名或重新创建帐户时，Signal 会在日志树（“分类账”）中记录更改，并通过前缀树（“索引书”）方便地通过日志树进行搜索。

sentences.en: Cloudflare and Trail of Bits each serve as independent auditors of these two types of trees, which together form the key transparency log.
sentences.zh: Cloudflare 和 Trail of Bits 各自充当这两类树的独立审计员，它们共同构成了关键的透明度日志。

blocks.html_en: All user data in the log is cryptographically obscured — public identifiers are processed through a verifiable random function and the values they map to are protected by a keyed hash function — so auditors never see any plaintext user data.

sentences.en: All user data in the log is cryptographically obscured — public identifiers are processed through a verifiable random function and the values they map to are protected by a keyed hash function — so auditors never see any plaintext user data.
sentences.zh: 日志中的所有用户数据都经过加密隐藏——公共标识符通过可验证的随机函数进行处理，它们映射到的值受到密钥哈希函数的保护——因此审计人员永远不会看到任何明文用户数据。

blocks.html_en: Your Signal app automatically and periodically checks your own public identifiers in this log, but verifying those of a connection must be initiated in the “View Safety Number” screen. All requests to look up identifiers in the log are unauthenticated, so they aren’t tied to a specific user account.

sentences.en: Your Signal app automatically and periodically checks your own public identifiers in this log, but verifying those of a connection must be initiated in the “View Safety Number” screen.
sentences.zh: 您的 Signal 应用程序会自动定期检查此日志中您自己的公共标识符，但验证连接的公共标识符必须在“查看安全号码”屏幕中启动。

sentences.en: All requests to look up identifiers in the log are unauthenticated, so they aren’t tied to a specific user account.
sentences.zh: 所有在日志中查找标识符的请求都未经身份验证，因此它们不与特定用户帐户绑定。

blocks.html_en: While we won’t dive into the implementation details in this post, interested readers can find them in our open-source repository, which was implemented based on an earlier draft of the IETF key transparency protocol and contains refinements to fit Signal’s use case.

blocks.html_en: Key transparency in practice today

sentences.en: Key transparency in practice today
sentences.zh: 当今实践中的关键透明度

blocks.html_en: Key transparency indicates that all devices in Signal’s ecosystem share the same view of the associations between an identifier and its public encryption key. It does not verify the identity of the user who controls a particular phone number or username. Concretely, this means that Alice and Bob can perform key transparency checks to ensure that they each have the right public key for a given account, but additional verification (such as following up after a Safety Number change) would still be necessary to detect a scenario where Mallory has fully taken control of Alice’s account.

sentences.en: Key transparency indicates that all devices in Signal’s ecosystem share the same view of the associations between an identifier and its public encryption key.
sentences.zh: 密钥透明度表明 Signal 生态系统中的所有设备对标识符与其公共加密密钥之间的关联共享相同的视图。

sentences.en: It does not verify the identity of the user who controls a particular phone number or username.
sentences.zh: 它不会验证控制特定电话号码或用户名的用户的身份。

sentences.en: Concretely, this means that Alice and Bob can perform key transparency checks to ensure that they each have the right public key for a given account, but additional verification (such as following up after a Safety Number change) would still be necessary to detect a scenario where Mallory has fully taken control of Alice’s account.
sentences.zh: 具体来说，这意味着 Alice 和 Bob 可以执行密钥透明度检查，以确保他们每个人都拥有给定帐户的正确公钥，但仍然需要进行额外的验证（例如安全号码更改后的后续操作）来检测 Mallory 完全控制 Alice 帐户的情况。

blocks.html_en: Today, your Signal app automatically verifies your own phone number and username data in the log. But to verify this for someone else, you need to have their phone number. Meaning that if you connected with someone on Signal via username, and did not exchange phone numbers or otherwise have access to their phone number, you will not be able to verify them.

sentences.en: Today, your Signal app automatically verifies your own phone number and username data in the log.
sentences.zh: 今天，您的 Signal 应用程序会自动验证日志中您自己的电话号码和用户名数据。

sentences.en: But to verify this for someone else, you need to have their phone number.
sentences.zh: 但要为其他人验证这一点，您需要知道他们的电话号码。

sentences.en: Meaning that if you connected with someone on Signal via username, and did not exchange phone numbers or otherwise have access to their phone number, you will not be able to verify them.
sentences.zh: 这意味着，如果您通过用户名在 Signal 上与某人联系，并且没有交换电话号码或以其他方式访问他们的电话号码，您将无法验证他们。

blocks.html_en: You probably have your Signal connection’s phone number if any of the following conditions are true:

sentences.en: You probably have your Signal connection’s phone number if any of the following conditions are true:
sentences.zh: 如果满足以下任一条件，您可能拥有 Signal 连接的电话号码：

blocks.html_en: • You started a Signal chat with this person using the “Find by phone number” option.

sentences.en: You started a Signal chat with this person using the “Find by phone number” option.
sentences.zh: 您使用“通过电话号码查找”选项开始与此人进行 Signal 聊天。

blocks.html_en: • You have this person’s contact saved in your phone’s address book (and they have opted to be discoverable by phone number in Signal).

sentences.en: You have this person’s contact saved in your phone’s address book (and they have opted to be discoverable by phone number in Signal).
sentences.zh: 您已将此人的联系人保存在手机的地址簿中（并且他们选择通过 Signal 中的电话号码来发现）。

blocks.html_en: • Your connection selected the option that lets everyone see their phone number in Signal (by default, nobody can).

sentences.en: Your connection selected the option that lets everyone see their phone number in Signal (by default, nobody can).
sentences.zh: 您的连接选择了允许每个人在 Signal 中查看其电话号码的选项（默认情况下，没有人可以）。

blocks.html_en: Keep in mind that Signal will only display a Signal connection’s phone number in the app if they are in your phone’s address book or if they have set their phone number visibility to everyone.

sentences.en: Keep in mind that Signal will only display a Signal connection’s phone number in the app if they are in your phone’s address book or if they have set their phone number visibility to everyone.
sentences.zh: 请记住，如果 Signal 连接的电话号码位于您手机的地址簿中或者已将其电话号码设置为对所有人可见，则 Signal 只会在应用程序中显示该电话号码。

blocks.html_en: It’s also possible for you to have an out-of-date phone number in the case that your connection on Signal changes their phone number. This action has no security impact on your connection’s public encryption key and the underlying encrypted messaging session. But it does mean that you will not be able to use automatic key verification for this connection because your phone will continue to have your connection’s old phone number which will no longer match the most recent phone number record in the ledger. This is similar to the situation described in the monitoring section where Bob sees a different address for Alice than what he had previously received. It’s very likely a legitimate change, but your device can’t distinguish that from server interference, and you should follow up with your connection through a secondary, trusted channel.

sentences.zh: 如果您在 Signal 上的连接更改了他们的电话号码，您的电话号码也可能已过期。

sentences.en: This action has no security impact on your connection’s public encryption key and the underlying encrypted messaging session.
sentences.zh: 此操作对您的连接的公共加密密钥和底层加密消息传递会话没有安全影响。

sentences.en: But it does mean that you will not be able to use automatic key verification for this connection because your phone will continue to have your connection’s old phone number which will no longer match the most recent phone number record in the ledger.
sentences.zh: 但这确实意味着您将无法为此连接使用自动密钥验证，因为您的手机将继续保留您连接的旧电话号码，该号码将不再与分类帐中的最新电话号码记录匹配。

sentences.en: This is similar to the situation described in the monitoring section where Bob sees a different address for Alice than what he had previously received.
sentences.zh: 这类似于监控部分中描述的情况，其中鲍勃看到爱丽丝的地址与他之前收到的地址不同。

sentences.en: It’s very likely a legitimate change, but your device can’t distinguish that from server interference, and you should follow up with your connection through a secondary, trusted channel.
sentences.zh: 这很可能是合法的更改，但您的设备无法将其与服务器干扰区分开来，您应该通过辅助的可信通道跟进您的连接。

blocks.html_en: As a privacy-focused default, we make automatic key verification unavailable in all of these cases and recommend that users use the existing safety number system, which allows users to manually verify that they share the same set of encryption keys with a specific connection by scanning a QR code or comparing a long verification number. Users who prefer not to rely on any third party, including Signal and the auditors, can disable the automatic key verification feature in the settings via “Privacy” > “Advanced” > “Automatic Key Verification” and continue to use manual safety number verification.

sentences.en: As a privacy-focused default, we make automatic key verification unavailable in all of these cases and recommend that users use the existing safety number system, which allows users to manually verify that they share the same set of encryption keys with a specific connection by scanning a QR code or comparing a long verification number.
sentences.zh: 作为注重隐私的默认设置，我们在所有这些情况下都无法进行自动密钥验证，并建议用户使用现有的安全号码系统，该系统允许用户通过扫描二维码或比较长验证号码来手动验证他们是否与特定连接共享同一组加密密钥。

sentences.en: Users who prefer not to rely on any third party, including Signal and the auditors, can disable the automatic key verification feature in the settings via “Privacy” > “Advanced” > “Automatic Key Verification” and continue to use manual safety number verification.
sentences.zh: 不想依赖任何第三方（包括 Signal 和审核员）的用户可以通过“隐私”>“高级”>“自动密钥验证”在设置中禁用自动密钥验证功能，并继续使用手动安全号码验证。

sentences.en: Conclusion

blocks.html_en: This work represents a significant collaboration within and outside of Signal, and we’re especially grateful to Cloudflare and Trail of Bits for serving as independent auditors. We thank them and the many other people in our ecosystem who make this work possible.

content_html_zh:
Signal 现在提供了一种称为“自动密钥验证”的功能，它补充了现有的安全号码系统。 信号始终是端到端加密的，自动密钥验证提供了一种额外的、简化的方式来确认您和端到端加密会话的另一“端”之间没有意外的一方。

它通过由您、您的 Signal 连接和第三方审核员执行的验证系统进行工作，这些验证系统共同提供与手动验证安全号码相同的保证。 与安全号码不同，这些验证是独立完成的，不需要面对面的会议或辅助沟通渠道。

该验证系统可确保电话号码或用户名与其公共加密密钥之间的关联在全球范围内保持一致，并且对 Signal 生态系统中的所有参与者都是透明的。 这可以防止在密钥所有者不知情的情况下更换密钥的情况 - 例如，如果恶意方破坏了 Signal 并将不同的密钥与您连接的电话号码相关联。

要查看此功能的实际效果，请转到 Signal 连接的配置文件，点击“查看安全号码”，然后点击“自动密钥验证”标题下的“自动验证”按钮。 当该功能可用且验证成功时，该按钮将显示绿色复选标记和“加密已验证”。 随着时间的推移，这种验证与您的 Signal 连接和第三方审核员不断执行的验证相结合，可确保该 Signal 连接密钥在整个 Signal 生态系统中的一致性。

此功能建立在称为“密钥透明度”的概念之上，我们将在本文的其余部分中使用该术语，因为我们解释了为什么我们构建了密钥透明度系统并对其工作原理进行了高级概述。

公钥和私钥入门

非对称加密技术使您能够向您的朋友发送只有您的朋友才能阅读的消息。 它涉及一对数学上关联的密钥，称为公钥和私钥，可用于多种应用，包括发送和接收消息。

想象一下，您有一个带槽位的上锁邮箱。 您的公钥就像您的邮箱地址 - 您可以与任何想要向您发送邮件的人共享它。 您的私钥就像邮箱密钥。 您是唯一拥有它的人，您可以用它来阅读发送给您的消息。 任何人都可以将邮件放入您的邮箱（使用您的公钥加密），但只有您可以解锁和阅读它（使用您的私钥解密）。 您的邮箱地址必须是公开的；如果没有人知道将邮件发送到哪里，您将无法接收邮件。

当您注册 Signal 时，Signal 应用程序会在注册过程中为您生成公钥/私钥对1。 私钥保留在您的设备上 — 只有您（Signal 或其他任何人）才能访问此私钥。 您的公钥将发送到 Signal，它充当所有用户公钥的中央目录。 当您想要向另一个 Signal 用户发送消息时，您可以向 Signal 询问您连接的公钥，并使用 Signal 返还的密钥和您的私钥对您的消息进行加密。

马洛里中路进攻

发送消息需要为接收者获取公钥，而获取公钥意味着依赖于中央目录。 从理论上讲，恶意目录操作员可以执行所谓的“中间 Mallory”攻击，尽管这样做需要外部人员绕过主要云提供商的安全性，或者需要特权内部人员故意针对特定帐户。 但即使这是一种非常先进且不太可能发生的攻击，我们仍然要防范。 我们将继续使用邮箱类比来说明这种攻击的假设工作原理。

假设鲍勃想要向他的朋友爱丽丝发送喝咖啡的邀请，因此鲍勃在中央目录中查找她的邮箱地址。 如果目录以某种方式被对手（Mallory）破坏，它可能会将 Bob 定向到 Mallory 的邮箱而不是 Alice 的邮箱。 当鲍勃将邮件发送到他认为是爱丽丝的邮箱时，它实际上会发送到马洛里的邮箱。 然后，马洛里使用她自己的邮箱密钥检索鲍勃的消息，阅读它，如果她选择修改它，将其放入新信封中，然后将其转发到爱丽丝的邮箱。

例如，在她的修改中，马洛里可以更改咖啡店位置或会议时间，导致爱丽丝出现在错误的地点或时间。 Alice 不会发现该消息已被拦截或篡改，因此对她来说，该消息看起来像是直接来自 Bob 的。 与此同时，鲍勃将徒劳地等待爱丽丝出现。 即使马洛里选择不更改鲍勃的消息，她阅读该消息的能力也构成了对通信隐私的严重侵犯。

关于咖啡的误解相对来说风险较低，但这种攻击在其他情况下可能会造成更大的伤害。

这种攻击之所以有效，是因为鲍勃从未真正验证过爱丽丝的地址。 鲍勃只是相信目录中列出的邮箱是她的，这是一个合理的假设。

但是，如果鲍勃想要格外谨慎，他可以通过面对面会议或某些次要的可信通信渠道直接向爱丽丝询问她的地址，如果爱丽丝和鲍勃是严格的笔友，这可能不可行。

那么，如果鲍勃无法亲自见到爱丽丝或使用辅助渠道，他如何验证爱丽丝的地址呢？

在这篇博文的其余部分中，我们将概述如何开发一个系统设计，使 Bob 能够自动验证中央目录中的数据，而无需直接与 Alice 通信。

设计密钥透明系统的类比

我们可以帮助 Bob 验证该目录是否具有 Alice 的正确地址的一种方法是保留对该目录所做的每次更改的记录。 如果有人更改了 Alice 在目录中的地址，它将被记录在这个按时间顺序排列的日志中，因此可以被检测到。 为了使这一点具体化，让我们扩展一下邮箱的类比。

假设一名职员在市邮局的公共账本中记录了每个人的地址变化。 每当有人获得新地址或更新现有地址时，店员就会在不断增长的账本背面添加一个新页面，并在那里记录地址更改。 办事员使用永久性记号笔来完成此操作，这样一旦写下某些内容，就没有人可以返回到页面并将其撕掉或修改其内容。 任何人都可以访问邮局并在分类帐中找到地址，包括他们自己的地址。

使用账本

对于任何给定的地址，邮局客户有两种方式与分类账交互：

  1. 像鲍勃这样的客户可以查找其他人（例如爱丽丝）的地址。
  2. 像 Alice 这样的客户可以查找自己的地址，以确保账本准确。

为了让鲍勃找到爱丽丝当前的地址，他必须从最后一页账本开始，一次翻回一页，直到找到爱丽丝的一页。 鲍勃从分类账的末尾开始向后工作，因为他想要爱丽丝的最新地址，而爱丽丝的地址可能随着时间的推移而改变。 随着越来越多的页面添加到分类帐中，这可能会成为 Bob 的大量工作，特别是如果 Alice 有一段时间没有更新她的地址，并且 Bob 需要筛选其他人的大量地址更改。

账本允许 Alice 验证她自己的地址是否正确列出，但为了做到这一点，她必须查看自上次访问以来的所有新页面，并检查它们是否没有错误地陈述她的地址。 和鲍勃一样，随着更多的页面添加到分类账中，这会变得很多工作。

如果爱丽丝和鲍勃生活在一个繁忙的城市，人们经常更换地址，那么他们都必须做大量的工作才能通过一次翻一页来使用分类帐。 我们需要一种更有效的方式让 Alice 和 Bob 与账本进行交互。

索引书介绍

在现实生活中，书籍通常包含按字母顺序排序的索引，使读者可以快速找到他们要查找的内容。 我们可以将同样的想法应用到我们的分类账中，通过在迄今为止地址已包含在分类账中的每个人的姓名上引入按字母顺序排序的索引簿。

当新页面添加到分类账以反映新地址或地址更改时，索引簿也必须更新，因此每当职员向分类账添加一页时，都会发布索引簿的新副本，其中包含截至该页面地址已包含在分类账中的人员集合。 这创建了一个巨大的图书馆，包含所有过去的索引书籍，可供公众使用。

现在，让我们假设爱丽丝和鲍勃总是查看账本任何给定页面的同一索引书。 在下一节中，我们将讨论系统的另一个组件，它允许 Alice 和 Bob 验证这个假设。

通过这种结构，鲍勃现在可以通过“二分搜索”策略更轻松地在账本中查找爱丽丝的地址，最好通过具体示例来说明这一策略。

假设一段时间内有 100 个新的或更新的地址，因此账本有 100 页，并且店员出版了 100 个不同版本的索引书。 为了简单起见，我们会说爱丽丝的地址只在她第一次搬到城镇时出现在账本中一次。

鲍勃首先翻到账本的中间。 然后他检查与该页面相关的索引簿。 索引书按字母顺序排序，因此很容易找到一个人的名字。 如果爱丽丝的名字存在于该索引书中，那么这要么是包含爱丽丝条目的索引书的第一版，要么是第一次出现在早期版本中，因此是分类帐中的早期页面。

无论哪种情况，Bob 都可以忽略账本的后半部分，并对账本的前半部分重复该过程，直到找到 Alice 地址发生更改的确切账本页面。 具体来说，当鲍勃找到两本相邻的索引书，其中第一本不包含爱丽丝的地址而第二本包含爱丽丝的地址时，他的搜索就会结束。

这个搜索过程有一些好处，第一个是它是高效的。 在一个有 10 亿页的账本中，鲍勃只需要检查最多 30 个不同的页面即可找到爱丽丝的地址，而不是向后翻转（在最坏的情况下）所有十亿页。 鲍勃的工作现在比以前轻松多了。

爱丽丝仍然想确保店员永远不会添加任何与她的地址错误的新页面。 然而，爱丽丝不需要检查每个账本和索引书。 她只需要检查鲍勃查看的相同地址即可找到她的地址，这确保了鲍勃为爱丽丝找到的地址已被爱丽丝本人验证。

这给我们带来了搜索过程的第二个好处，即当 Alice 和 Bob 查看具有相同页数的账本时，它是确定性的。 如果店员在鲍勃和爱丽丝的搜索之间添加更多页面，事情会变得更加复杂，但主要思想保持不变。 在一个有十亿页的账本中，爱丽丝可以遵循与鲍勃相同的搜索过程，检查鲍勃检查过的相同页面，并确保其中没有一个包含有关她地址的错误信息。

通过同意搜索账本的流程，爱丽丝和鲍勃建立了一种与账本交互的方式，使他们能够切实实现各自的目标。 随着账本不断增长，Bob有一种有效的方法来找到Alice的地址，而Alice也有一种有效的方法来确保Bob找到的地址是准确的。

为了清楚起见，这个类比被简化了。 实际上，Alice 可以多次更新她的地址，并且支持这种搜索需要在索引簿中存储更多的数据，而不仅仅是姓名。 我们构建了一个开源密钥透明度服务器，将这些相同的想法应用于信号消息传递。

那办事员呢？

到目前为止，我们描述的搜索过程就好像 Alice 和 Bob 亲自翻阅账本页面并检查索引簿一样。 在实践中，这是不现实的，因为账本和索引簿太大，爱丽丝或鲍勃无法直接处理。 相反，爱丽丝和鲍勃要求店员代表他们进行搜索并报告结果。

但邮局可能会受到像马洛里这样的对手的影响，马洛里冒充职员，并希望最终欺骗鲍勃，让他认为爱丽丝的地址实际上是马洛里的家。 因此，Alice 和 Bob 不能简单地信任店员；他们必须能够自己独立验证搜索过程。

为此，他们要求店员交回店员在搜索过程中查看的特定分类账页和索引簿中的所有数据，然后他们自己仔细检查结果。

只有当办事员交回的数据可信时，双重检查才有效，这就提出了一个明显的问题：如果马洛里冒充办事员对记录所说的内容撒谎怎么办？ 例如，马洛里可以维护一个秘密的第二个分类账，记录爱丽丝的错误地址，或者为同一分类账页发布两个不同版本的索引书。 Mallory 可以向 Alice 提供一个视图的数据，向 Bob 提供另一个视图的数据，欺骗他们验证所提供的数据，而不会意识到 Mallory 的欺骗。

爱丽丝和鲍勃需要一名独立证人来保证店员的诚实。

第三方审核员

为了防止 Mallory 向 Alice 和 Bob 提供不同的数据，他们依赖第三方审计员。 这些审计员就像公证人一样，在职员将每个连续的页面添加到分类帐并发布相应的索引书版本时监视着职员。

他们检查索引簿的每个版本是否包含与前一版本相同的所有数据（只有一个条目除外），并且审核员没有删除或以其他方式秘密修改分类账中的任何先前页面。 如果这些条件成立，审计员会在分类账页和索引簿上签名，表明记录已正确添加。

审计员只会在每一页和索引簿上签名一次，因此，如果职员试图向 Alice 和 Bob 展示第 50 版索引簿的不同版本，则职员只能为其中一个版本提供有效的随附审计员签名。 通过检查和验证这些审计员签名，爱丽丝和鲍勃可以确信职员正在维护一个分类帐和相应的一组索引簿，因此他们正在查看同一组记录。

对于 Signal 关键透明度的实施，Cloudflare 和 Trail of Bits 充当值得信赖的第三方审计员。

监控

第三方审计员确保店员向 Alice 和 Bob 提供同一组数据，但他们无法验证记录数据的准确性。 例如，Mallory 可以尝试向分类帐添加一个页面，列出 Alice 的虚假地址更改。 从审计师的角度来看，只要马洛里正确添加新的分类账页并发布新版本的索引书，这就是合法的更改。 然而，当鲍勃在账本中查找爱丽丝的地址时，他会发现这个假条目并相信这是爱丽丝的真实地址。

这就是监控发挥作用的地方。 回想一下，客户有两种方式与账本交互：查找别人的地址，以及查找自己的地址。 监控要求 Alice 和 Bob 定期执行这两件事，每个都检测不同类型的篡改。

Alice 通过定期查找和验证她最近的地址记录来监控她自己在分类账中的数据。 如果她发现一个意外的地址，她应该通过第二个可信渠道提醒鲍勃，他为她收到的地址不可信。

鲍勃还必须定期查找爱丽丝的最新地址，并检查它是否与他之前收到的地址相符。 这很重要，因为在插入虚假地址更改后，马洛里可以尝试通过稍后添加恢复爱丽丝正确地址的条目来掩盖她的踪迹。

值得注意的是，从鲍勃的角度来看，为爱丽丝找到不同的地址看起来与合法的地址更改相同，这是更常见的解释。 尽管如此，他还是应该通过辅助渠道向爱丽丝确认她确实搬家了。 如果她不这样做，他应该将之前的地址视为不可信。

Alice 定期进行自我检查，Bob 按照自己的时间表检查账本，因此两者都不能保证在发生 Mallory 干扰时立即发现。 但这两种监控与第三方审核相结合，形成了一个完整的检测系统：审核保证 Alice 和 Bob 正在查看相同的数据，监控保证他们都定期检查数据的准确性。 他们共同确保马洛里的篡改最终会被发现。

将其绑定回 Signal

那么，这一切如何与 Signal 中的关键透明度联系起来呢？

在 Signal 中，您可以选择通过电话号码或用户名（如果您选择创建用户名）来发现。 如果您决定通过电话号码或用户名被发现，其他人可以在 Signal 中输入您的号码或用户名来发起消息请求。 Signal 存储一个中央目录，最终将这些公共标识符映射到用户的公钥，就像我们邮箱类比中的“名称”和“地址”一样。

当 Signal 用户注册、更改电话号码或用户名或重新创建帐户时，Signal 会在日志树（“分类账”）中记录更改，并通过前缀树（“索引书”）方便地通过日志树进行搜索。 Cloudflare 和 Trail of Bits 各自充当这两类树的独立审计员，它们共同构成了关键的透明度日志。

日志中的所有用户数据都经过加密隐藏——公共标识符通过可验证的随机函数进行处理，它们映射到的值受到密钥哈希函数的保护——因此审计人员永远不会看到任何明文用户数据。

您的 Signal 应用程序会自动定期检查此日志中您自己的公共标识符，但验证连接的公共标识符必须在“查看安全号码”屏幕中启动。 所有在日志中查找标识符的请求都未经身份验证，因此它们不与特定用户帐户绑定。

虽然我们不会在本文中深入探讨实现细节，但感兴趣的读者可以在我们的开源存储库中找到它们，该存储库是基于 IETF 密钥透明度协议的早期草案实现的，并包含适合 Signal 用例的改进。

当今实践中的关键透明度

密钥透明度表明 Signal 生态系统中的所有设备对标识符与其公共加密密钥之间的关联共享相同的视图。 它不会验证控制特定电话号码或用户名的用户的身份。 具体来说，这意味着 Alice 和 Bob 可以执行密钥透明度检查，以确保他们每个人都拥有给定帐户的正确公钥，但仍然需要进行额外的验证（例如安全号码更改后的后续操作）来检测 Mallory 完全控制 Alice 帐户的情况。

今天，您的 Signal 应用程序会自动验证日志中您自己的电话号码和用户名数据。 但要为其他人验证这一点，您需要知道他们的电话号码。 这意味着，如果您通过用户名在 Signal 上与某人联系，并且没有交换电话号码或以其他方式访问他们的电话号码，您将无法验证他们。

如果满足以下任一条件，您可能拥有 Signal 连接的电话号码：

  • 您使用“通过电话号码查找”选项开始与此人进行 Signal 聊天。
  • 您已将此人的联系人保存在手机的地址簿中（并且他们选择通过 Signal 中的电话号码来发现）。
  • 您的连接选择了允许每个人在 Signal 中查看其电话号码的选项（默认情况下，没有人可以）。

请记住，如果 Signal 连接的电话号码位于您手机的地址簿中或者已将其电话号码设置为对所有人可见，则 Signal 只会在应用程序中显示该电话号码。

如果您在 Signal 上的连接更改了他们的电话号码，您的电话号码也可能已过期。 此操作对您的连接的公共加密密钥和底层加密消息传递会话没有安全影响。 但这确实意味着您将无法为此连接使用自动密钥验证，因为您的手机将继续保留您连接的旧电话号码，该号码将不再与分类帐中的最新电话号码记录匹配。 这类似于监控部分中描述的情况，其中鲍勃看到爱丽丝的地址与他之前收到的地址不同。 这很可能是合法的更改，但您的设备无法将其与服务器干扰区分开来，您应该通过辅助的可信通道跟进您的连接。

作为注重隐私的默认设置，我们在所有这些情况下都无法进行自动密钥验证，并建议用户使用现有的安全号码系统，该系统允许用户通过扫描二维码或比较长验证号码来手动验证他们是否与特定连接共享同一组加密密钥。 不想依赖任何第三方（包括 Signal 和审核员）的用户可以通过“隐私”>“高级”>“自动密钥验证”在设置中禁用自动密钥验证功能，并继续使用手动安全号码验证。

结论

密钥透明度提供了一种易于使用的方式来确认消息安全的重要部分，补充了我们现有的安全号码系统。
